title: Yasmina Reza knows what’s up with art! #theatre #broadway #jamescorde...
transcript: Putting James Corden, Neil Patrick Harris and Bobby Cannavale on stage together in a Broadway show was always gonna be a bit of a divisive move. But I hope the naysayers aren't totally dismissing this Tony winning play. This week I finally caught the Broadway revival of the play Art which has been running for a couple months now. For those who don't know, it's about this group of three friends, and one of them spends $300,000 on this painting that is basically all white. And it sparks this very passionate debate, not only about the subjectivity of art, but also about the complicated ways we perceive our friends and their behaviors. I actually really enjoyed this play when I saw it about 9 years ago in a remount of the original staging. And funny enough, my memory of that production was that it was extremely funny, but kinda lightweight. And ironically, it was kind of the reverse for me this time; the themes actually struck some very personal chords for me, but meanwhile, I barely laughed throughout. Comedically, it didn't feel as sharp or organic all around. And I think Neil Patrick Harris and Bobby Canavale in particular felt a bit miscast. Not necessarily because they weren't believable as these people, but I don't think the material was playing to their strengths. James Corden, by contrast, actually felt quite a bit more at home in the role and the material. Probably the most compelling performance of the three, but predictably, it also sometimes crossed the line into overdoing it As an ensemble, I also don't think they were all that cohesive. I didn't necessarily buy them as people who had been friends for 25 years. And in general, I feel like they could have used a bit more directional guidance. I think even the emotional or relatability factor that I mentioned earlier had less to do with the production and more to do with it just being a good play and seeing it again after a bit more life experience. For a play that's presented in this kind of straightforward, lightweight format, it's deceptively profound. And even though it takes it to a sort of comedic and dramatic extreme, it explores dynamics that feel so true to life but are rarely depicted in media. And I think I picked up on a lot of those insights last time, But they didn't stick with me as much as how much the play made me laugh. And I guess this time, I didn't really have that problem.
